requirements.observable: With db = TinyDB(path) (default JSONStorage): record os.stat(path).st_ino, call db.insert({'a': 1}); the inode at path has changed (the file was replaced, not rewritten in place) and json.load(open(path))['_default'] == {'1': {'a': 1}}. A spy wrapping os.replace/os.rename sees a call whose destination is the database path and whose source is a different (temporary) file. After inserting many documents and then removing most of them, json.load of the file succeeds and equals the current data (no leftover bytes from the longer old contents).

requirements.statement: The database file on disk is always either the complete old version or the complete new version, never half-written: if the process dies or the write fails part-way (e.g. the disk fills up, an OSError such as ENOSPC/EFBIG while the new contents are being written, or any other error before the swap completes), the file at the database path is byte-for-byte the previous version and still loads with its previous data.

evidence.quote: so the file on disk is always either the old version or the new one
if the process dies or the disk fills up in the middle of a write, the JSON file is left half-written

requirements.observable: Populate a DB and save the file bytes, then make the next write fail part-way and check that the file is byte-identical to the saved bytes and TinyDB(path).all() returns the old documents: (a) in a subprocess, ignore SIGXFSZ and set resource.RLIMIT_FSIZE slightly above the current file size, then insert a document large enough to exceed it (simulated full disk; an in-place rewrite leaves a truncated, unparsable file); (b) patch os.replace and os.rename to raise OSError so the swap fails; (c) insert a non-JSON-serializable value. (d) SIGKILL a subprocess in the middle of a large write (e.g. from a hook called during the write): afterwards the file parses and equals either the full old or the full new data.

requirements.statement: After a write has been swapped into place, the same JSONStorage/TinyDB instance keeps working on the new file: subsequent reads through that instance return the newly written data (not the stale contents of the replaced file), and successive writes build on each other without losing earlier updates. A TinyDB opened afterwards on the same path also sees the latest data.

evidence.quote: the JSON file is left half-written and the whole database becomes unreadable
so the file on disk is always either the old version or the new one

requirements.rationale: Swapping a new file into place means the database path refers to a different file after every write, while the current implementation works through an open file handle (seek to 0, write, truncate). If reads kept going through a handle to the replaced file they would return stale data and later writes would drop earlier ones, i.e. the database would be broken. The user only asks to change how writes are performed and wants the database to stay readable.

requirements.statement: The temporary file is created on the same filesystem as the database file (e.g. in the database file's directory), so the swap is a single atomic rename that works regardless of where the system temp directory is; the write must not degrade into a non-atomic copy over the database file.

requirements.rationale: A rename/replace is only atomic within one filesystem; a temporary file in the system temp directory would make the swap fail with a cross-device error or fall back to copying over the database file in place, breaking the guarantee that the file is always either the old or the new version.

requirements.statement: Writes do not leave temporary files behind: after a successful write the temporary file has become the database file, and when a write fails with an exception (e.g. disk full while writing the temporary file, or an error during the swap) the partially written temporary file is removed, so the database's directory contains the same files as before the write.

In every case the listing is unchanged (only the database file).

requirements.statement: A write that cannot be completed is reported to the caller: if writing or swapping the temporary file fails, JSONStorage.write (and therefore the TinyDB operation that triggered it, e.g. insert/update) raises an exception instead of returning normally as if the data had been saved.

requirements.statement: The new contents are completely written, flushed and fsync'ed (os.fsync or os.fdatasync) to the temporary file before it is swapped into place, so the swap never installs a file whose data has not reached the disk, and errors that only surface on flush/fsync (e.g. a full disk) abort the write before the database file is replaced.

instruction:
Make the following changes:
- JSONStorage.write no longer rewrites the database file in place (seek to 0, write, truncate): it writes the complete new serialized contents to a temporary file and then swaps that file into place over the database path with an atomic rename/replace (e.g. os.replace). After a successful write the database file contains exactly the new serialized data (also when the new contents are shorter than the old ones).

The following existing behaviour must be preserved:
- The database file on disk is always either the complete old version or the complete new version, never half-written: if the process dies or the write fails part-way (e.g. the disk fills up, an OSError such as ENOSPC/EFBIG while the new contents are being written, or any other error before the swap completes), the file at the database path is byte-for-byte the previous version and still loads with its previous data.
- After a write has been swapped into place, the same JSONStorage/TinyDB instance keeps working on the new file: subsequent reads through that instance return the newly written data (not the stale contents of the replaced file), and successive writes build on each other without losing earlier updates. A TinyDB opened afterwards on the same path also sees the latest data.
- Apart from how the file is written, existing JSONStorage/TinyDB behaviour is preserved: every option the base JSONStorage supports keeps working as before (e.g. create_dirs, encoding, access_mode, extra json.dumps keyword arguments such as indent/sort_keys), the text written to the file is the same as the base implementation produces (same json.dumps arguments and encoding), a storage opened read-only (where the base supports access_mode='r') still refuses writes with an IOError/OSError without modifying the database file, relative database paths such as TinyDB('db.json') work, and the repository's existing test suite still passes.
- Writes do not leave temporary files behind: after a successful write the temporary file has become the database file, and when a write fails with an exception (e.g. disk full while writing the temporary file, or an error during the swap) the partially written temporary file is removed, so the database's directory contains the same files as before the write.
- A write that cannot be completed is reported to the caller: if writing or swapping the temporary file fails, JSONStorage.write (and therefore the TinyDB operation that triggered it, e.g. insert/update) raises an exception instead of returning normally as if the data had been saved.
- The new contents are completely written, flushed and fsync'ed (os.fsync or os.fdatasync) to the temporary file before it is swapped into place, so the swap never installs a file whose data has not reached the disk, and errors that only surface on flush/fsync (e.g. a full disk) abort the write before the database file is replaced.

Constraints:
- The temporary file is created on the same filesystem as the database file (e.g. in the database file's directory), so the swap is a single atomic rename that works regardless of where the system temp directory is; the write must not degrade into a non-atomic copy over the database file.
- Repository code is never run directly on the host machine; tests and Python snippets are run only through the provided wrappers /home/user/cs_workspaces/CS-02/run_tests.sh [pytest args] and /home/user/cs_workspaces/CS-02/run_python.sh -c '...', which execute the code in an isolated container.
- All work stays inside /home/user/cs_workspaces/CS-02: the change is made in the git working copy of TinyDB at /home/user/cs_workspaces/CS-02/tinydb, and no files outside /home/user/cs_workspaces/CS-02 are created or modified.
